topics.title: Membrane transport
topics.summary: The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer that controls what enters and leaves the cell. Small non-polar molecules cross on their own; ions and large polar molecules need proteins. Transport is either passive (down the concentration gradient, no ATP) or active (against the gradient, uses energy).
key_points: Simple diffusion: small non-polar molecules (O₂, CO₂) pass straight through the bilayer.
Facilitated diffusion: channel or carrier proteins help ions and polar molecules move down their gradient, with no ATP.
Osmosis: water moves from lower to higher solute concentration across a partially permeable membrane.
Active transport: pumps move substances against their gradient using ATP, e.g. the Na⁺/K⁺ pump (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in).
Endocytosis and exocytosis move large particles in vesicles.
topics.example: Glucose enters red blood cells by facilitated diffusion through GLUT1 carrier proteins: down its gradient, so no ATP is needed.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between passive and active transport?
flashcards.back: Passive goes down the gradient with no ATP; active goes against it and uses energy (ATP).
3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ in, per ATP.

flashcards.front: Which molecules can cross the bilayer by simple diffusion?
flashcards.back: Small, non-polar molecules such as O₂ and CO₂.

questions.q: Which process moves substances against their concentration gradient?
questions.explanation: Only active transport moves substances from low to high concentration, and it needs energy, usually ATP.

why_tempting.1: Facilitated diffusion uses proteins like active transport does, but it still only moves substances down the gradient.

questions.q: Which of these crosses the phospholipid bilayer most easily without a protein?
questions.explanation: Small, non-polar molecules like O₂ dissolve through the hydrophobic core of the bilayer.

why_tempting.0: Na⁺ is small, but it's charged, and charged particles can't pass through the hydrophobic core.

questions.q: A drug blocks ATP production in a cell. Which process stops first?
options: Diffusion of CO₂ out of the cell
questions.explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump is active transport and depends directly on ATP. The others are passive.

why_tempting.3: GLUT1 is a protein, but it's a carrier for facilitated diffusion, which needs no ATP.

questions.q: A red blood cell is placed in pure water. What happens?
options: It swells and may burst as water enters
Nothing, as water can't cross membranes
questions.explanation: Pure water has a lower solute concentration than the cell, so water moves in by osmosis and the cell can burst (lysis).

why_tempting.0: That happens in a concentrated (hypertonic) solution, which is the opposite situation.

questions.q: Inside a cell, Na⁺ is low and K⁺ is high. Which statement best explains how this is kept stable?
options: Na⁺ and K⁺ diffuse freely until they're balanced
The Na⁺/K⁺ pump uses ATP to pump 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, against their gradients
Osmosis carries ions with the water
Facilitated diffusion moves Na⁺ out and K⁺ in
questions.explanation: Keeping ions away from equilibrium needs constant energy input. The pump does this, and the gradient it makes also powers other transport, like Na⁺–glucose co-transport.

why_tempting.3: Facilitated diffusion can only move ions down their gradients, so it would undo the gradient, not keep it.

topics.title: Mitosis vs meiosis
topics.summary: Mitosis makes two genetically identical diploid cells for growth and repair. Meiosis makes four genetically different haploid gametes through two divisions. Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes; meiosis II separates sister chromatids.
key_points: Mitosis: 1 division → 2 identical diploid (2n) cells.
Meiosis: 2 divisions → 4 different haploid (n) cells.
Meiosis I separates homologous pairs, so the cells are already haploid after meiosis I.
Crossing over (prophase I) and independent assortment (metaphase I) create variation.
Count chromosomes, not chromatids, to decide haploid vs diploid.
topics.example: Humans: 2n = 46. After meiosis I, each cell has 23 chromosomes, each still made of 2 chromatids. After meiosis II, each gamete has 23 single chromosomes.

flashcards.front: How many cells, and what ploidy, after meiosis?
What separates in meiosis I? In meiosis II?
flashcards.back: Meiosis I: homologous chromosomes. Meiosis II: sister chromatids.

questions.q: How many cells does meiosis produce from one cell?
questions.explanation: Meiosis has two divisions, so 1 → 2 → 4 cells.

why_tempting.0: Two cells is the result of mitosis, or of meiosis I alone.

questions.q: At the end of meiosis I, are the two cells haploid or diploid?
questions.explanation: Meiosis I separates homologous pairs, so each cell has one set of chromosomes (n), even though each chromosome still has two chromatids.

why_tempting.0: Each chromosome still has two chromatids, so the DNA amount looks 'double', but ploidy counts chromosomes, not chromatids.

questions.q: A cell with 2n = 8 completes meiosis I. How many chromosomes does each new cell have?
questions.explanation: Homologous pairs separate, so 8 → 4 chromosomes per cell (n = 4), each still with 2 chromatids.

why_tempting.0: 8 would be the answer after mitosis, which keeps the chromosome number the same.

questions.q: Which event makes the cells from meiosis genetically different from each other?
questions.explanation: Crossing over swaps sections between homologous chromosomes. Together with independent assortment, it creates new combinations of alleles.

why_tempting.0: DNA replication copies DNA exactly, so it doesn't create new combinations.

questions.q: A student says: 'Mitosis and meiosis II are basically the same.' Which is the best evaluation?
options: Wrong: meiosis II separates homologous pairs
Partly right: both separate sister chromatids, but meiosis II starts with haploid cells and the chromatids aren't identical after crossing over
Right: they're exactly the same process
Wrong: meiosis II doesn't separate anything
questions.explanation: Both separate sister chromatids, but meiosis II starts with haploid cells, and crossing over means the sister chromatids are no longer identical.

why_tempting.2: The mechanics look the same, which is why it's tempting, but the starting cells and the genetic outcome differ.

topics.title: Cellular respiration
topics.summary: Cellular respiration releases energy from glucose to make ATP. Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm; the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix; the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane, where most ATP is made and oxygen is the final electron acceptor.
key_points: Glycolysis: cytoplasm; glucose → 2 pyruvate; net 2 ATP; no oxygen needed.
Link reaction and Krebs cycle: mitochondrial matrix; release CO₂ and make NADH and FADH₂.
Electron transport chain: inner mitochondrial membrane; makes most of the ATP by oxidative phosphorylation.
Oxygen is the final electron acceptor and forms water.
Without oxygen, cells use fermentation to regenerate NAD⁺ (lactate in animals).
topics.example: During a sprint, muscles run short of oxygen and switch to lactate fermentation. It's fast, but gives only 2 ATP per glucose.

flashcards.front: What is the final electron acceptor in the ETC?

flashcards.back: The inner mitochondrial membrane, by the electron transport chain and ATP synthase.

questions.explanation: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, which is why even cells without mitochondria can do it.

why_tempting.0: Most of respiration happens in the mitochondria, but glycolysis comes first, outside them.

questions.q: What is the final electron acceptor in the electron transport chain?
questions.explanation: Oxygen accepts the electrons at the end of the chain and combines with H⁺ to form water.

why_tempting.0: NAD⁺ accepts electrons earlier, in glycolysis and the Krebs cycle, not at the end of the chain.

questions.q: Cyanide blocks the electron transport chain. What happens to ATP production?
options: It falls sharply, leaving only the small amount from glycolysis
questions.explanation: Most ATP comes from oxidative phosphorylation. Without the ETC, only glycolysis (with fermentation) still makes a little ATP.

why_tempting.3: Glycolysis doesn't depend on the ETC, so it's the part that keeps going.

questions.q: Why do muscle cells make lactate during intense exercise?
options: To make more ATP than aerobic respiration
To regenerate NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue without enough oxygen
Because lactate is the final electron acceptor in the ETC
questions.explanation: Without enough oxygen, NADH builds up. Turning pyruvate into lactate recycles NAD⁺ so glycolysis can keep making 2 ATP.

why_tempting.0: Fermentation is faster, but it makes far less ATP per glucose than aerobic respiration.

questions.q: Which statement correctly links each stage of respiration to its location?
options: Glycolysis: matrix; Krebs: cytoplasm; ETC: outer membrane
Glycolysis: cytoplasm; Krebs: matrix; ETC: inner membrane
Glycolysis: inner membrane; Krebs: matrix; ETC: cytoplasm
All stages happen in the matrix
questions.explanation: Cytoplasm → matrix → inner mitochondrial membrane. The folded inner membrane (cristae) gives a large surface area for the ETC.

why_tempting.0: Mixing up 'matrix' and 'cytoplasm' is the most common error here, so link 'glycolysis' with 'outside the mitochondria'.

topics.title: Organelles
topics.summary: Eukaryotic cells contain membrane-bound organelles, each with a job. The nucleus holds DNA; ribosomes make proteins; the rough ER and Golgi process and ship proteins; mitochondria make ATP; lysosomes break down waste.
key_points: Nucleus: stores DNA; the nucleolus makes ribosomes.
Rough ER: has ribosomes; makes and folds proteins for export.
Golgi apparatus: modifies, packages and sends proteins in vesicles.
Mitochondria: aerobic respiration and ATP.
Lysosomes: digestive enzymes that break down waste and old organelles.
topics.example: Pancreas cells that secrete digestive enzymes have lots of rough ER and Golgi, because they make and export so much protein.

flashcards.back: Modifies, packages and sends proteins in vesicles.
Rough ER has ribosomes and makes proteins; smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies.

questions.q: Which organelle packages proteins into vesicles for secretion?
questions.explanation: The Golgi modifies and packages proteins, then sends them out in vesicles.

why_tempting.2: Lysosomes are made from Golgi vesicles, but they digest material rather than package proteins for export.

questions.q: A cell secretes a lot of protein hormone. Which organelles would you expect it to have in large amounts?
questions.explanation: Protein for export is made on the rough ER, then processed and shipped by the Golgi.

why_tempting.0: Smooth ER makes lipids, which matters for steroid hormones, but not for protein hormones.

questions.q: Put the path of a secreted protein in the correct order.
options: Ribosome on rough ER → rough ER → vesicle → Golgi → vesicle → cell membrane
questions.explanation: It's made on ribosomes on the rough ER, folded in the ER, carried to the Golgi in a vesicle, modified there, then sent to the membrane in a secretory vesicle (exocytosis).

why_tempting.0: Both organelles are right, but the order is reversed: the ER always comes before the Golgi.
